rv.q: Million Dollar Quartet, arriving in the West End after making a splash in America, is just such an exercise in upbeat nostalgia.
The musical – first staged in 2006 and seen in the West End in 2011, now newly transferred from Cirencester’s Barn theatre – is a curious mix of wildly fanciful and diligently factual.

It strikes a clever balance between documenting and dramatising a moment in history, commenting on the nature of fame, legacy, and how music continues to evolve with the times - while also unabashedly having fun with it.

Distinct vocal styles, wonderful harmonies, virtuoso guitar and piano playing, nifty moves (credit to choreographer Joanna Goodwin) and compelling storytelling combine to give us a rare window into their lives.

Staged as an impromptu jamming session, the performance is filled with recognisable songs that you are encouraged to bounce along to, with each singer delivering their own work as well as joining in as musicians and backing vocalists on the others.

The production works best when it embraces itself as an exuberant celebration of 1950s music: joyful, nostalgic and irresistible, but attempts to add greater historical or dramatic weight instead expose thin characterisation, particularly for Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash.
A hugely enjoyable evening, packed with talent, charm and plenty of toe tapping moments.
Million Dollar Quartet captures the essence of this remarkable story with creativity, energy and real flair.
Highly recommended, brilliantly sung and played show!
The production delivers a polished theatrical experience without losing the spontaneity that is so central to its premise.
These committed central performances ensure that there is a whole lot of shaking going on in the auditorium and audiences are sent home on an invigorated high.
This combination of a lively cast, impressive musicianship, and atmospheric design makes this show feel like a living piece of rock ’n’ roll history.
In O’Boyles' production, having such a talented cast turns what could just be a cliché Rock ‘n’ Roll night into a real show.
What it does offer is an enjoyable exploration of what might have happened on a particular night at the birth of a musical revolution.
It is pure, unadulterated theatrical joy.
Quite simply, Million Dollar Quartet is a superbly realised juke box musical that is not only fun, it will nourish and sustain you.
Million Dollar Quartet is a pitch‑perfect explosion of nostalgia, talent and sheer rock ’n’ roll magic.
The incredible talent in this show had the entire opening night audience on their feet.
With exceptional live musicianship, a catalogue of iconic songs and a scene-stealing performance from Joe Bence as Jerry Lee Lewis, this is rock ’n’ roll theatre played with infectious energy.
Million Dollar Quartet offers a rare opportunity to feel like a fly on the wall for a rare moment in the genre’s history.

While Million Dollar Quartet never dives deep into its plot and the audience never receives more than a few snippets of biographical information about the four stars, it nevertheless succeeds in delivering precisely what its audience wants: wonderful deliveries of some of the most famous hit songs from the 50s.
Million Dollar Quartet is a really fun night out, with plenty of opportunity to sing and dance alongside some of the most famous singers in musical history.

Million Dollar Quartet is a musical that is put together nicely, whilst act 1 and 2 don't quite connect with each other, it's nevertheless a cheery show for the most part, with nice performances, excellent music and it's for the fans of these stars.
A supremely talented cast rescue this paint by numbers jukebox musical nostalgia fest
And so, Million Dollar Quartet is just an overpromiser that bets all its prospects of success on the work of others without doing anything by itself.

cn.t: Critics praise the electrifying performances and authentic rock 'n' roll energy, with audiences dancing in the aisles. However, some find the thin plot and jukebox format lacking substance beyond the stellar musicianship and nostalgic appeal.
